objective: count in tenths.
approach:
To begin this lesson, display the Explore task and ask students to look at the whole brownie. How many small pieces can the brownie be cut into? Then ask them how many pieces each character will get.
Show them that if the brownie is cut into 10 pieces, then each piece is 1 out of 10 pieces. How do we write 1 out 10? If students do not recall fractions previously learnt, write the fractional notation 1/10 as you read 1 out of 10, and then tell students it is read as 1 tenth. Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and ask students where to place 1/10. Give them time to discuss this, and then ask them if they know how many tenths there are in 1 whole. Count together with them using the number line. Ask them what 2 pieces of brownie is — 2/10 — and then indicate this on the number line. Work through Master until you reach 1 whole, and then count the tenths backwards. Count forwards and backwards a few times, starting from different tenths. Explain that the number line is divided into intervals, each representing 1 tenth.
During Guided Practice, students are exploring different visuals of tenths in a bar and on a number line. What are the similarities between them? Are there any differences?
formative_assessment:
identify a tenth as 1 of 10 equal pieces.
Students can use a number line to show tenths.
Students can count in tenths.
Students can complete a number sequence by counting in tenths.
Students can use concrete materials to show tenths.

objective: add fractions with the same denominator within 1 whole.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and discuss the number of parts the cake has been divided into. How many pieces have strawberry icing? How many pieces have chocolate icing? Therefore, we can see that 3 pieces of cake with strawberry icing and 5 pieces of cake with chocolate icing make a total of 8 pieces. Ask students how we write 3 out of 8 pieces. Tell them we read 3/8 as 3 eighths. What about 5 out of 8 pieces? How do we read 5/8? Point out that 3/8 and 5/8 will make 8/8.
Ask students what they notice about the denominators and numerators. Guide them to see that the denominator tells us the total number of equal parts a whole has been divided into; that is why it remains the same whether we count the strawberry or chocolate parts. The numerator tells us the number of equal parts we are counting, and that is why it is 3 when we count the strawberry parts and 5 when we count the chocolate parts.
Provide students with small paper squares in two different colours and ask them to combine them to make 8 pieces. For each pattern, ask them to write the two fractions that will make 8/8. Show them that we can also use number bonds to present the pairs of fractions.
During Guided Practice, students are finding number pairs to make a fraction.
formative_assessment:
count in fractions.
Students can use concrete materials to show fractions.

objective: add fractions with the same denominator within 1 whole.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a piece of paper that has been divided into fifths. Tell them to pretend that this is a sushi roll. Show them the Explore task and ask them to share the bar in the same way. Ask them how they will do this; allow them to shade the parts and cut them out, etc. Then ask them to display what they have done and show you how much of the sushi roll has been eaten by each character.
Ask them to write the fraction for the amount of sushi each character has eaten. Guide them to see that as the sushi roll has been divided into 7 parts, each part should be written as 1/7 and read as 1 seventh. Then ask them to find how much sushi both of them have eaten altogether. Show them we can add the two fractions: 1/7 and 3/7 to find the total amount of sushi eaten, which is 4/7.
Guide students to conclude that adding fractions with the same denominator is the same as adding whole numbers. We do not add the denominator because it only tells us how many equal parts a whole has been divided into. We add the numerators because they tell us the number of equal parts we are counting.
During Guided Practice, students are adding together fractions with the same denominator using pictures and fractional notations.
formative_assessment:
Students understand the relationship between the numerator and denominator.

objective: add fractions with the same denominator within 1 whole.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a piece of paper and ask them to fold it into 6 equal pieces. Also provide them with two different coloured pencils. Tell them that the paper has been cut into 6 equal pieces.
Now show students the Explore task and ask them if they can solve the problem using their own paper. Allow them some time to work out the solution. When they begin to say they have taken all the paper, tell them that is impossible because they were only taking a fraction of it! Tell them they will need to prove it to you. Ask them if they are able to draw it for you, as in Master 1. Can they show you using a bar? Finally, agree that all the paper has been taken.
Ask students if this is true for all fractions — when the numerator equals the denominator, do you have 1 whole? Ask them to try this out with a number of fractions to check that it is always correct. Provide the class with further examples of addition as shown in the Master tasks.
During Guided Practice, students are adding fractions with the same denominator.

objective: subtract fractions with the same denominator within 1 whole.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with an enlarged copy of the sushi roll in the Explore task and discuss the problem with them. There are two parts to the problem. The first part of the problem tells us that Hannah has already taken 1 piece of the sushi roll, and the picture shows the amount of sushi left. The second part tells us that Ravi is going to take 5 more pieces of sushi.
Ask students how many pieces the sushi roll was divided into at first. How can we tell? Since Hannah has taken 1 piece and there are 8 pieces left, this tells us that there were 9 pieces at first. Ask students what the fraction is for 1 piece of sushi roll, and tell them that 1/9 should be read as 1 ninths. What fraction of the sushi has Hannah taken? 1/9 should be read as 1 ninths. What fraction of the sushi roll is left after Ravi has taken his share? 3/9 should be read as 3 ninths.
Ravi then takes 5 pieces. What fraction of the sushi roll is 1 piece? There are 8/9 of the sushi roll remaining. After he takes 5/9, what fraction of sushi roll is left? Ask students if they know which calculation to do to find the fraction of sushi left. We need to use subtraction to find the fraction of sushi roll left: 8/9 – 5/9 = 3/9.
Go through Master 2, subtracting 3/7 from 6/7. Guide students to conclude that subtracting fractions with the same denominator is the same as subtracting whole numbers (as in addition). We do not subtract the denominator as it tells us how many parts a whole has been divided into. We subtract the numerators as they tell us the number of parts we are counting.
During Guided Practice, students are subtracting fractions with the same denominator.

Students understand the relationship between the numerator and denominator.

objective: recognise and show equivalent fractions.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a number of paper strips of equal length. Ask them to take a piece of paper and fold it into 2 equal parts, shading in 1 part. Tell them the shaded part is their piece. Ask them what fraction they have, prompting them to see it is 1 half. Write 1/2 on the board and place a strip of paper divided into 2 parts beside it.
Now show students the Explore task and ask them to discuss what is meant by this problem. How can we have more parts, but still use the same strip of paper? Is there something we can do to increase the number of parts here? Prompt students to fold the paper more times. Is it possible to turn the 2 parts into 4 parts? Allow them time to attempt this. Now that we have 4 parts, what should we call each part? We call them 1 quarter. Ask students if they know how to write the fraction for 1/4, and then write it on the board and place a strip of paper divided into 4 parts beside it.
Ask students to compare the two strips of paper — compare each part and compare the whole. Ask them to tell you what they observe. The whole has remained the same, but the number of parts has changed. Lead students to see that 1/2 is now 2/4 by putting the two strips one above the other to compare. Guide them to see that although the whole has been divided into more equal parts, the whole has not changed. We call these fractions equivalent because they are equal, so 1/2 = 2/4. Ask them to try finding other equivalent fractions of 1/2.
During Guided Practice, students are expected to divide the images into smaller parts, paying close attention to which number is being given: the numerator (the number of parts that will be shaded) or the denominator (the number of parts that the whole has been divided by).
formative_assessment:
Students understand that the numerator is the number of equal parts from a whole that is being counted.
Students understand that the denominator is the total number of equal parts a whole has been divided into.
Students understand that equivalent fractions are equal.

objective: recognise and show equivalent fractions.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with strips of paper and ask if they are able to fold them into 4 equal pieces. Ask students to shade in 1 part and ask them the name of that part, reminding them that the name of a whole piece, which has been separated into 4 equal pieces, makes quarters. Then show students the Explore task.
Ask them if they think it is possible to write 1 quarter in different ways. Could folding the paper be helpful, as in the last lesson? Allow them some time to work on this, taking their answers and creating a chart of possible solutions. Are they able to turn the 4 equal pieces into 8 or 16, or any other number? How many pieces are shaded in each? Does this mean they are then equal to 1/4?
During Guided Practice, students are looking at a fraction diagram and determining whether or not fractions are equivalent. Notice the variation in the horizontal and vertical layouts, as well as the fact that 4 is a common number. Help students navigate through complications, for example, working out that 4 shaded parts do not make fractions equivalent.

objective: recognise and show equivalent fractions.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with several strips of paper, and then show them the Explore task.
As they begin folding, tell them your friend said if you place a number line above or below the folded paper and make markers at each of the folds, you can place the fractions on a number line. Is this true? How might that look? Let students try this in their exercise books or on a whiteboard. Model this for them on a large piece of paper and ask them what would go at the start of the number line. Is it the number 1, or is it 0?
Allow students to discuss which number they think would go at the start of the number line and why. Tell them your friend said that he pretends a number line is just like the measures on the side of a measuring cup. When there is no water in the measuring cup, there is 0.
As you begin to fill the cup, what happens? Can you use this information to help construct a number line? It is important for students to see the folded paper above or below the number line so they can see the relationship between the folded sections on the paper and the fractions. Ask students if, by looking at the chart you have collectively created, they can see equivalent fractions.

approach:

objective: find equivalent fractions.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide each student with an enlarged copy of the fraction in the Explore task. Ask them what is 2/3. Where is 2/3 shown on the bar model? Guide students to see that the whole is divided into 3 parts, each part is 1 third and the 2 coloured parts make 2/3. It is read as 2 thirds. Ask them what they understand by sixths. What does it tell us about the whole? It means that a whole is divided into 6 equal parts. How can we write 2/3 as sixths?
Provide students with diagrams of bar models divided into 3 equal parts and allow them some time to work on this. Guide them by asking how 3 parts can be converted into 6 parts. How do we get 6 from 3? Can we use multiplication? Allow students to work on this problem together. When structuring their learning, review the multiplication method and picture-splitting method learnt in previous lessons. Continue with the same procedure using the examples from Master.

objective: find equivalent fractions.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide each student with a bar model diagram divided into 5 parts and ask them to shade 3/5. Now show students the Explore task and ask them how many tenths are equal to 3/5? What does it mean when the numerator changes from 3 to 6? It means that we have change the 3 parts into 6 parts. How can we do that?
Allow students time to draw on their bar models. Let them show their drawing and explain their thinking. Ask them if the whole still remains as 5 parts? If we divide 3/5 into 10 smaller parts, we must do the same for all the fifths. How many parts is the whole now? How many parts are shaded? We can see that 3/5 = 6/10.

objective: find the simplest form of a fraction.
approach:
Prepare a game similar to the one in the Explore task for this lesson using 9 small pieces of rectangular paper.
To begin the lesson, show students the the Explore task and ask them how many parts have been painted altogether. What fraction is each part? Holly paints 3 parts. What fraction does she paint? Holly paints 3/9 of the game. Use Master and the pre-prepared game to show the class 3/9. Then move the parts to show that 3 parts (3/9) can form 1 part, and 9 pieces (9/9) can form 3 parts. We can see that 3/9 = 1/3 of the game. When we do this, we say that 1/3 is the simplest form of 3/9.
Repeat the process for the fraction of the game Sam paints (6/9). In order to demonstrate the simplest form, it is easier to show the fractions of game the children paint using the ways shown in Master.
During Guided Practice, students are using a picture to help them see the simplest form of a fraction. Encourage them to draw diagrams to help them answer the second set of questions if needed.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them how they will know which fractions are equivalent to 4/12. Give them time to look at the shaded bars. Which fractions are equivalent to 4/12? There are 2 fractions: 2/6 and 1/3.
Follow Master to structure students' responses, starting first with 2/6. Ask them whether they notice anything special between 4/12 and 2/6, and allow them to discuss. Ask them to use multiplication and division to show the special relationship. Do the same for 4/12 and 1/3. Then show students that 4/12 = 2/6 = 1/3. We say that 1/3 is the simplest form of 4/12.

objective: compare fractions with the same denominator.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask them to read the problem and look at the diagram. Charles takes 1 tenth and Tama takes 9 tenths. Who has more? Students will be able to easily see that Charles has less pancake. Ask the students to look at the fractions and guide them to see that Charles takes 1 part from 10 parts. So 1 out of 10 parts becomes 1/10. Ask the students to find other fractions that show that Tama has a greater fraction of the cake than Charles. What fraction does Charles have when Tama has a greater amount? What do they notice about the numerator and denominator?
Then represent the fractions using a bar model, as shown in Master 1. We can see that 1/10 is less than 9/10. Therefore, Charles has less pancake than Tama. Help students to see that when the denominators are the same, we only need to compare the numerators to see which fraction is greater.
For the next part of the task, ask students if there are other ways for Tama to take more of the pancake than Charles. What if Tama gets 7 pieces? What would the fraction be for Tama? What about Charles? Show students Master 3 and ask students what fractions are shown for Charles and Tama. Both get 5/10, therefore they get the same amount. Ask students to write 5/10 in its simplest form. 5/10 = 1/2.
Lastly, show students Master 4 and ask them what fractions are shown for Charles and Tama. Tama gets 2/10 and Charles gets 8/10. Who gets more? 8/10 > 2/10. Ask students to write these two fractions in their simplest form: 4/5 > 1/5.
During Guided Practice, students are comparing fractions with the same denominators.

objective: compare fractions with different denominators.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them how they can compare fractions with different names. Is this possible? Tell students your friend said she uses pictures to compare fractions that do not have the same name. Would this be helpful? Draw a bar model to show sixths, and then another one to show sevenths. Ask students how to shade the bar to show 5/6 (shade 5 parts out of 6). What about 5/7 (shade 5 parts out of 7)? By comparing the sizes of the shaded parts in each bar, students will be able to see that 5/7 is less than 5/6.
Ask students to compare 2/3 and 2/5 using the same method. Allow them time to draw the bars to make the comparison. Then ask students to compare 4/5 and 4/9 by looking at the number lines in Master 3. Ask students to use >, < or = to compare the two fractions.
During Guided Practice, students are comparing fractions with different denominators by shading the bar models and comparing number lines. For Guided Practice 3, ask students to try drawing their own bar models to make the comparison.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them what fraction of eggs are in the picture; is it quarters or sixths? How can we know? Allow students time to discuss the problem and find a solution. Ask them how many ways they can show you the answer, e.g. with pictures, numbers or words. Guide students to conclude that the concepts for subtraction of fractions are the same as subtraction of whole numbers, e.g. taking away, crossing out or counting backwards.
Provide students with further examples, as in Master. Once they have solved the problem, ask whether the fraction that remains is in its simplest form. How do they know? Ask them to show you using pictures.

approach:

Students can see from the picture that 5 pieces of puzzle have been put together and Holly is holding 1 piece. Therefore, the puzzle has 6 pieces. We can write 1 = 6/6.
Ask students to write the fraction for the amount of the puzzle Holly has completed. Ask them to think about the calculation and how they would show the solution. Structure the learning for this task by asking students to represent this problem and solution in as many ways as possible (pictures, fractions, words, number lines, and so on). Students have to learn how to rewrite 1 as a fraction with different fractional parts to do the subtraction.
During Guided Practice, students are subtracting fractions from 1 whole by rewriting the 1 as a fraction.

objective: recognise, find and write fractions of a discrete set of objects.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with 8 counters each. Show them the Explore task and ask them to solve the problem using the counters. If there are 8 jelly beans in total shared equally between 2 friends, how many will each get? Ask students to use their counters to show that each child will get 4 jelly beans. Then ask them if it is possible to represent this as a fraction.
Explain that another way of sharing 8 jelly beans with 2 children is to find 1/2 of 8. Show the class how the 8 counters can be divided into 2 parts by drawing 2 halves within a bar model, each half with 4 counters. Guide students to see that there are 2 halves and 1/2 of 8 is 4. How can we write that down mathematically? Show them how to write the mathematical statement, 1/2 of 8 = 4. Explain that when we share a set of objects with 2 people, we need to divide it into 2 parts and find how many are in 1 part and this is the same as finding 1/2 of the set of objects.
What if we need to share the 8 jelly beans between 4 children? What fraction of the 12 jelly beans are we finding? What if we need to share 8 jelly beans between 4 children? What fraction of the 8 jelly beans are we finding? Guide students to draw the quarters and eighths within a bar model and divide the counters accordingly. Then write the mathematical statements for each problem.
During Guided Practice, students are using bar models and pictures to show how to share equally using fractions. At this stage, allow them to continue using the counters from the original task.

divide a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number.

objective: recognise, find and write fractions of a discrete set of objects.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with 12 counters each and show them the Explore task. Ask if they are able to work out what 3/4 of the children is. How about finding 1/4 first? Can they use what they learnt in the previous lesson to find 1/4 of 12? Ask them to use the counters to show how to divide 12 by 4. Then ask them again what is 1/4 of 12. Reiterate that 1/4 means 1 part out of the 4 parts. After they have shown the divided counters, ask them to write the mathematical statement 1/4 of 12 = 3.
If we can see that 1/4 is 3 children, what will 3/4 be? If 1/4 is 1 part of 12 children, then 3/4 would be 3 parts of 12 children. We can use multiplication, 3 × 3 to find that 3/4 is 9 children. Ask students to write the mathematical statement 3/4 of 12 = 3 × 3 = 9. Explain that when we have to find the multiple parts of a set of objects, we can first find 1 part, and then multiply to find the answer.
Then ask students to try finding 2/3 of 12 children and 5/6 of 12 children. Can they write the mathematical statements for these problems? Guide students to use the counters and draw the fractions to find the answers, and then relate it to the mathematical statements they need to write.
During Guided Practice, students are finding the fractions of a set of objects. Reinforce the idea that they need to find 1 part before finding 2, 3 or 4 parts to find the answer. Allow them to use counters to do the division and multiplication.

objective: relate fractions to division.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask how they would share one marshmallow twist. How can it be equally divided between 2? Ask students what they would do.
Structure the learning as represented in the Master tasks. To share 1 marshmallow twist between 2 children, we have to divide it into 2 equal parts. Each child gets 1 part. Write the mathematical statement 1 ÷ 2 = ? Ask students how to write 1 part out of 2 parts, and then write 1/2 on the board and say that each child will get 1/2 of 1 marshmallow twist. Draw a number line on the board indicating 0 and 1. Ask students if they know where 1/2 would be, and ask them to show you 1/2 on the number line. Guide students to see that 1/2 is the same as saying 1 ÷ 2.
What if you had a whole sandwich to share among 4 children? How would you share it equally? How should we divide the pizza? How much would each child get? Can they draw the sandwich to show this? Can they write a mathematical statement for this? Can they show this using a number line? Guide students to see that 1/4 is the same as saying 1 ÷ 4, and then ask them to work on Master 3 in the same way. Lead them to see that any whole number, when divided by another whole number, can be expressed using fractions.
During Guided Practice, students are being asked to divide a number and 1. For the first task, guide students to use the fractional notation for division of whole numbers (8/2).

objective: relate fractions to division.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and allow them to discuss whether Ruby and Tama have the same amount. Tell them your friend said that they do because Ruby's waffle is cut into 3 equal pieces and 2 of them are on her plate, which shows 2 thirds. Is this true? What about Tama? Does he have thirds? How do we know? How is each whole divided, is it into 6 or into 3? Allow students to discuss this idea.
Structure the lesson working through the Master tasks. For Master 2, ask students how they would show you their thinking using pictures. If there were 3 whole waffles that need to be shared between 4 children, then how would we cut them? Ask them to draw this and explain it to one another. Guide students to relate fractions to division: when 3 is shared by 4 children, they have divided 3 wholes into 4 equal parts each. Each child will get 3/4, so 3 ÷ 4 is the same as 3/4.
During Guided Practice, students are relating fractions to division. In the first example, there are 9 whole sandwiches being shared among 3 children: 9 ÷ 3. They have to relate the problem to 9/3. In the second example, there are 4 whole sandwiches being shared between 5. How should the sandwiches be sliced? Does each child get an equal amount of each sandwich? In this case, they need to relate it to 4/5.

objective: relate fractions to division.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with 2 circular pieces of paper to fold and cut/shade. Show them the Explore task and ask how they would share 3 pancakes equally between 2 children. Allow students time to show you using the paper provided. Remind them that if there are 2 children, the pancakes should be divided in a way so that each gets their fair share. Prompt students to draw what they have allocated to each child from each pancake: halves. Then work through Master and show the class how each child will get 1 1/2 by using paper cutouts to share the pancakes equally: each child gets one whole pancake and half of the third pancake.
Look at Master 2. If 5/4 has a numerator that is larger than the denominator, then what would this look like in a drawing? Give students some time to work this out. Reinforce the fact that the denominator tells us how many parts a whole has been divided into. If 1 whole is divided into 4 parts, and there are 5 parts, it means we have to draw 1 whole with all the parts shaded, and another whole with 1 of its parts shaded to show 5/4. We can also rewrite 5/4 as 1 whole and 1/4. Using the cutouts, reassemble the 5 pieces of pancake to show this.
During Guided Practice, students are sharing whole numbers equally between children, and arriving at answers that equal more than 1.

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with strips of paper that can be used as bar models. Show them the Explore task and discuss the problem, helping them identify the information given. Tell them your friend said it cannot be solved because you don't know how many bananas and oranges Amira bought. Is this true? Are there clues to help us? How can we know?
